claims.text: Successful formation of homogeneous noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles is governed by synchronization of precursor reduction rates through a tailored thermal profile.
A rapid heating-and-cooling cycle can cause the constituent elements to reduce simultaneously.
Concurrent reduction causes elemental nuclei to form concurrently.
Limiting atomic diffusion or free-atom mobility favors random alloy formation.
Sequential reduction of different precursors can produce phase-separated noble-metal HEA nanocrystals.
Sequential reduction causes uncontrolled nanoparticle morphology.
The proposed synthesis begins with a solid, uniformly mixed multimetal precursor on a support or in a homogeneous mixture.
The controlled intervention is a high-heating-rate, short-dwell pulse followed by fast cooling, compared with a slower or prolonged thermal ramp.
Precursor composition, concentration, support, and other synthesis conditions are held constant while thermal-treatment parameters are changed.
Rapid, simultaneous reduction creates a high density of nucleation sites.
Rapid reduction freezes a random high-entropy configuration and produces a homogeneous single-phase alloy.
Shortening the processing time restricts atomic diffusion and atom rearrangement.
Rapid thermal treatment forces all constituent elements to reduce nearly concurrently.
Rapid thermal treatment minimizes differences among the reduction potentials of the constituent precursors.
Restricted surface mobility prevents segregation and phase separation.
The optimized fast thermal profile will yield a homogeneous solid-solution structure with uniform elemental distribution.
The optimized fast thermal profile will preserve high surface-atom exposure.
The slower or longer-dwell baseline will show more phase separation or elemental segregation than the fast-profile sample.
The mechanism applies to solid mixed noble-metal precursors when thermal reduction kinetics determine mixing, but may not apply to purely solution-based reduction.
Failure of the fast treatment to produce significantly greater single-phase homogeneity than the slower control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis treats synchronized reduction as the condition favoring homogeneous alloying, yet the boundary excludes systems whose constituent reduction potentials are nearly identical, even though such similarity should favor synchronization rather than invalidate the proposed mechanism.

The baseline language broadly associates sequential reduction with segregation, while cited same-system evidence reports that five-element noble-metal HEAs can form a single phase even when the elements reduce consecutively. The hypothesis does not delimit this documented exception, weakening its stated governing role.
